en: The *Caturādhyāyī* of Śaunaka: Om, salutation to Sarasvatī;
Om, salutation to the Brahma-Veda.

Atharvāṅgirasa [states]: "Of the four classes of words—nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles—the two qualities of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) and metrical verse (*padya*) are established by convention (*prātijñam*).
Likewise, the usage 'here' (*iha*) and so forth is obtained optionally (*vibhāṣā*) in a general sense."
3. A final syllable is *padya*. 4. A vowel other than *ṛ* and *ḷ* is *padya*. 5. Also, the letter *l* and the *visarjanīya* are *padya*.

The first and last *sparśas* [are not elided]; nor is the *ca*-group [elided]. According to Śaunaka’s formal proposition (*pratijñāna*), words ending in the first [consonant] of a class take the third [consonant of that class]; however, this is not a rule of application (*vṛtti*).
9. And [the letters] produced by greater contact; 10. the second and fourth [consonants of each class] are aspirated; 11.
the final [consonants of each class] are nasalized.
In unvoiced consonants, the articulation is breath;
in voiced vowels, it is resonance. A syllable uttered with equal effort and at a high pitch is called udātta (acute).
15. A low tone is the anudātta (unraised). 16. An accented syllable that is thrown back [onto the preceding] is the svarita (circumflex). 17.
The first half-mora of a svarita is udātta (raised).
The specific locations within the mouth for the articulators are as follows: 18. For those produced in the throat, it is the lower part of the throat;
19. For those of the jihvāmūlīya class, it is the root of the jaw.
For palatals, the middle of the tongue;
for cerebrals, the tip of the tongue turned back;
for the letter *ṣ*, the *droṇikā* [the middle of the tongue].
For dentals, the tip of the tongue is spread out; for labials, the lower lip;
for nasals, the nose.
The articulation of nasal sounds is through both the mouth and the nose (27);
that of the letter *r* is at the roots of the teeth (28); and the mode of articulation for the stops (*sparśa*) is by complete contact (*spṛṣṭa*) (29).
The semi-vowels (antasthā) are slightly contacted (īṣatspṛṣṭa),
the sibilants (ūṣman) are widely opened (vivṛta),
and so too are the vowels (svara).
Some [hold that] the *e*-vowel and *o*-vowel are most opened (*vivṛtatama*), and the *ā*-vowel is even more so than those. 33–35.
The vowel *a* is closed (saṃvṛta); 36. the letter *r* and the vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ* are touched (saṃspṛṣṭa); 37.
the first mora of long and protracted vowels [is open]. 38.
The *salakāra* is the vowel *ḷ*.

(39) Diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) are sounds that are touched together (*saṃspṛṣṭa*); their occurrence is as if they were a single sound. (40) [This does not apply] to the substitution of the places of articulation for *e* and *o*. (41)
The visarjanīya is called abhiniṣṭāna (42).
Abhinidhāna is the retention of a consonant; it is pressed, more nasalized, and characterized by diminished breath and sound (43).
There is abhinidhāna of a stop before another stop (44).
And [the doubling occurs] at the end of a word and in the avagraha; 45. [the doubling] of the letter *l* before sibilants (*ūṣman*); 46. [the doubling] of *ṅ*, *ṇ*, and *n* before the letter *h*. 47.
And that which is established [is the first]; 48. other than this is the conjunct; 49. half the measure of the preceding form is the subsequent common constituent (samānakaraṇa). 50.
A short vowel is light when followed by a consonant cluster (51); any other [vowel] is heavy (52), as is a nasalized vowel (53).
54. Also at the end of a word. 55. Consonants [are doubled] before a following vowel. 56. The first member of a conjunct consonant [is doubled] before a preceding vowel.

And the *padya* [is formed] by the sequence of the letter *ra* and the letter *ha* (57); and [the vowel] produced by the sequence [of these] is the long [vowel] (58); the short [vowel] has one *mātrā* (59).
And consonants;
a long vowel has two morae,
and a protracted vowel has three morae.
In the words *ṣaṭ* and *puruṣa*, the final syllable becomes *ur*; and in the words *daśan* and *dāśa*, the initial [consonant] is replaced by a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*).
(63) In the root *kṛp*, the letter *r* is replaced by *l*. (64) This does not apply to *kṛp* and others. (65)

The letter *ra* replaces the *la* in words such as *pāda*, *maṅguli*, and so forth. (66) When *na* or *ma* is elided, the preceding [consonant] becomes nasalized. (67) And this also occurs when a *yaṇ* [consonant] undergoes the substitution of a sibilant (*ūṣman*). (68)

69. And when there is a single substitution [of *a*] with the preceding vowel for a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*), [the rule applies]. 70. In the case of a pause (*avasāna*), as in *puruṣa ā babhūvān*.
71. That which follows the letter *r* after an *ṛ*-vowel [is subject to the following rule].
The vowel *u*, when it is an *apṛkta* (uncombined),
becomes long and is also treated as *pragṛhya*. The vowels *ī* and *ū* are also *pragṛhya* when they stand in the sense of the locative case.
The two dual endings (dvivacanāntau), the vowel *e* (ekāraḥ),
and the words *asme*, *yuṣme*, *tve*, and *me* are acute-accented (*udāttāḥ*).
78. These [words] are plural; 79. a particle not joined [with another word] and lacking the vowel *ā*;
80. as well as one ending in the vowel *o*.

81. When addressed, [the final vowel] is elided, except in Vedic usage. 82. In *ārtnī* and similar words, the following [consonant] is doubled. 83. A short vowel at the end of a word becomes nasalized.
The long vowel [is substituted] in the neuter plural;
[the substitution of *ū* for the penultimate vowel occurs] in the case of *pāṃsu*, *māṃsa*, and others;
[the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel occurs] in the case of the roots *han* and *gam* when followed by the suffix *san*.

87. [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after words ending in *śam*, *māndya*, and those ending in a vowel; 88. [it is applied] after a word ending in *vasu* when it occurs in a five-word compound (*pañcapadyā*);
89. [it is applied] after a word ending in the suffix *īyas*.
90. [The term *vī* is used] for that which follows a consonant. 91. [The term *puṃs* is used] for a masculine noun. 92. The penultimate letter, preceding the final consonant, is called the *upadhā*.
A vowel is a syllable (93).
Before an aspirated consonant, the preceding [consonant] becomes non-aspirated (94).
The application [of phonetic changes] occurs according to internal proximity (95).
In *khaṇvakhā3 i* and *khaimakhā3 i*, the vowel *i* at the beginning is unaccented (*anudātta*). 96.
97. "Ābabhūvām" and "itīta" [are examples where] the vowel *e* is not protracted (*apluta*). 98. Consonants that are not separated by vowels constitute a conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
99. Within the same word, following a non-final stop (*sparśa*), the final stops are replaced by their respective nasal counterparts (*yama*) according to their order.
After the letter *ha*, [the svarabhakti] occurs with the nasal (*nāsikya*);

after the letter *ra*, when followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*) that is itself followed by a vowel, there is a svarabhakti equal to half an *a*-vowel, though some say it is a quarter; when followed by any other consonant, it is a quarter or an eighth.
That same [svarabhakti] is called *sphoṭana*.
The preceding vowel and the non-interruption of the conjunction [of consonants]. 104.
*khaṇvakhā3 i khaimakhā3*
In the midst of this, may that desire of yours be fulfilled— *idā3 idā3*— thus,
being uplifted, it is now released. *A3*.
O Sūrya, have you been created?
The Person has pervaded all the quarters;
he has eaten the porridge facing away.
ḥ! "Pratyañcā3m" (toward yourself)— thus you have eaten the rice.
"Having eaten with porridge," [he said];
"I desire it, I desire it."
Thus,
that which was then—
this indeed is it.
Thus, there are one hundred and five protracted vowels (*pluta*).
And thus ends the first chapter of the *Caturādhyāyikā* within the *Saṃhitā*.
Among the final consonants that are not *anuttama*, the third letter [of each varga] is substituted before voiced consonants and vowels;
(2) at the end of a word, unvoiced consonants [are substituted]; (3) and [the same applies] before unvoiced consonants. (4)
5. An *uttama* [stop] before *uttama* [stops].
6. A second [stop] before *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*. 7. Before those [consonants], the fourth [stop] preceding them replaces *h*.
8. After the letter *ṭ*, [the same letter] is substituted for *s* and *t*. 9. After *ṅ*, *ṇ*, and *n*, [the respective letters] *k*, *ṭ*, and *t* are substituted before *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*. 10.
Before the letter *ś*, *ñ* is substituted for *n*.
11. Before a voiced consonant of the *ca*-group, [the *ya* of *yaval*] becomes the corresponding nasal; 12. before a *ṭa*-group consonant, it becomes *ṇa*;
13. before *śa* and *la*, it becomes the corresponding place of articulation for the letter *ta*.

14. Also before the *ca*-group and *ya*, [the preceding *s* becomes *ṣ*]. 15. By those two [rules], when they are in the same word (*samānapada*), a dental (*tavargīya*) [is substituted] for the preceding [sound].
16. After the letter *ṣ*, [this occurs] even when they are in different words (*nānāpada*).
The letter *ś* follows a member of the *tavarga*;
there is elision (*lopa*) of the *ś* [of the root *śās*] after *udaḥ* in the case of the roots *sthā* and *stambh*;
and [there is elision] of the *repha* (the letter *r*) when followed by a *repha*.

From an excellent *sparśa*, [the following] *anuttama* [nasal] occurs before an *anuttama*; (20) [this also applies] when a vowel or the like follows [the *anuttama*] at the end of a word. (21) There is no [substitution] of *va* after the letter *a*. (22)
And [the forms] *gaviṣṭau* and *gaveṣaṇaḥ* [are also examples].
(23) According to Śākaṭāyana, there is the substitution of a breath (*leśavṛtti*) after an aspirated stop (*adhisparśa*).

(24) When a stop (*sparśa*) that is voiceless (*aghoṣa*) and not followed by a sibilant (*anūṣmapara*) follows, the *m* of the word *pum̐s-* becomes *visarjanīya*, except in the case of [words] beginning with *apuṃs-* and others. (25)
The *visarjanīya* replaces the *nakāra* when followed by voiceless consonants of the *ca*, *ṭa*, or *ta* classes, provided they are not followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*).
(26) In the case of words such as *upabaddha*, the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s* before a vowel when preceded by the vowel *ā*.
(27) In the phrase *vṛkṣāṃ vanāni*, [the *m*] is replaced by *r* before the letter *v*. (28)
The *ṛ* of words such as *ṛtūn*, *ṛtsṛjate*, and *vaśī*, when preceded by a nasal, [is changed to *l*]; 29. not so for words such as *samairayant*; 30.
a *m* followed by a stop is changed to the stop of its own place of articulation; 31.
There is elision of [the final *n*] before internal spirants (ūṣman) within a word; 32. [This elision occurs] only before spirants when they are internal to a word; 33.
And [this applies] to the letter *n*; 34.

When both [consonants] are *l*-sounds, the *l* is nasalized. (35) It is not [nasalized] before *r*, *j*, or *t*. (36) And also not before a *v* that arises from a euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*). (37)

In the reversal of classes, there is *sphoṭana* (explosion), provided there is a pause with the preceding [sound]. 38. There is no [transition] of the *ṭa*-class into the *ca*-class; however, when a temporal separation occurs here, they call that *karṣaṇa* (attraction). 39. The *visarjanīya* takes the place of the following sound when it is voiceless. 40.
41. A *yakāra* [is substituted] for [the final consonant of a word ending in] a vowel.
42. A *repha* [is substituted] for the final consonant of a word ending in a vowel when followed by a nasal (*nāmin*).
43. And [a *repha* is also substituted] when followed by a voiced sound (*ghoṣavat*).

The suffix *ka* is applied after the word *vara*, and the suffix *bha* is applied after a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). (44) [The word] *dvār* is derived from the root *vṛ* with the suffix *a*. (45) [The word] *ahar* is derived from the root *hā* with the suffix *a*. (46)

When one [word] is addressed, the dual ending is obtained for that which ends in the plural; furthermore, the final [vowel] of words ending in *san* and *uta*, as well as those consisting of a single vowel (*svaravyaya*), is elided. And [the same applies to] *svarṣāḥ*.
50. The word *ahar* is neuter.
51. [The substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan-*,] however, does not occur when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), nor in the words *nūpara*, *rātri*, and *rathantara*.
52. [The substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan-*,] as well as [the substitution of *ūdhas-* for *ūdhar-* and *bhūs-* for *bhavas-*], occurs before the suffixes *am* and *nu*.
The vowel *u* replaces the vowel following *a* when followed by *a* (53),
and also when followed by a sonant consonant (54).
The vowel following *ā* is elided (55).
Like a salutation that causes the penis to bristle, [he approached] the tree. This is that [tree] in its manifestation; he did not stumble.
In the case of *dīrghāyutva* and so forth (59),
the letter *u* in the word *dura* becomes a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) before the root *dāś*,
and the letter *t* is heard [in its place] (60–61).
In a compound, the letter *s* [is changed to *ṣ*] when it follows *ka* or *pa*, provided it is not internal to a word; this applies to the *sadyaḥ-śreyaḥ* group and in Vedic meters.
(62) The words *niḥ*, *dur*, and *āviḥ* [change their final *i* to *ṣ*] even when not in a compound. (63) The word *triḥ* [is similarly treated]. (64)
The suffix *ku* is applied after the words *kuru*, *kara*, *kṛt*, *kṛṇotu*, *kṛti*, and *kṛdhi* when they refer to one's own ears (*svakarṇayoḥ*).
(65) Then, the suffix *ra* is applied after those same words when they refer to Brahman (*brahmapare*).
(66) The suffix *ra* is also applied after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyāḥ*) when it denotes a limb of the body (*aṅgebhyaḥ*), with the exception of the group beginning with *pari*. (67)
68. [The suffix *kvin*] is applied after [the root *sac*] when it occurs with *divaspṛthivī*, except when followed by *varjam*.
69. And [it is applied] after [the root *sac*] when it occurs with *pṛṣṭha*.
70. [The suffix *kvin* is applied] after [the root *pati*] when it means "lord of these cows," except when followed by *para*.

71. [The substitution of] *ī* occurs for the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when it is not followed by *aśaci*. 72. [The substitution of] *ī* occurs for the word *iḍā* when it is in the locative case (*pade*). 73. [The substitution of] *ī* occurs for the word *pitṛ* when it is in the locative case (*pitari*).
And *dyauḥ* [is used] in the first case; *āyuḥ* [is used] in the first case; *pre* [is used] before words meaning "to steal" (*muṣi*) and "to live" (*jīva*).
Paridhiḥ patātau (77), nivataḥ spṛṇatau (78), manaspāpe (79).

And in *rāyaspoṣa* and similar forms, there is a *ṣ* for a palatal (*nāmī*) penultimate vowel (80); here, there is a *ṣ* for a palatal penultimate vowel (81); [and] for *sah*, when it has become *sāṭ* (82).
83. When a secondary suffix (taddhita) beginning with *t* follows, [the substitution of] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occurs, except for those [forms] beginning with *taiḥ*, *tvam*, and *aham*.
84. And [this applies] also when [suffixes] beginning with *tat*, *tān*, and *grā* follow.
86. [The substitution of *s* for *ś* occurs] in the case of *stṛta*, *svasṛ*, and *svapiṣu*.
87. [The substitution of *s* for *ś* occurs] for the *sakāra* (the letter *s*) of an affix following a name ending in *repha* (*r*). 88. [The form] *straiṣūyam* [is derived by this rule].
Even when there is elision of *n*,
[the augment *ṭi* is added] after a prefix (*upasarga*) before a verbal root (Pāṇini 6.1.91), and also after a reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) (Pāṇini 6.1.92).
92. [The suffix *kvanip* is added] after the roots *sthā*, *hi*, *si*, and *ci*, even when there is an intervening *a*.
93. [The suffix *kvanip* is added] after the root *sthā*, even when there is an intervention by the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
94. [The suffix *kvanip* is added] after the words *parama* and so forth, except in the sense of "cooking" (*pāka*).
And with the two hands turned away from the right (aprasavya);
95. [The rule applies] to the *stoma* and *soma* of the fire;
96. [the suffix] *suj*; 97. [is applied].

98. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the group beginning with *try*. 99. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the root *sad* when preceded by an *ṛ*-vowel. 100. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *barhis*, *pathin*, *ap*, *su*, *div*, and *pṛthivī*.
101. After the roots *hi*, *div*, and *as*, [the suffix *ktvā*] takes the augment *iṭ*.
102. [The augment *iṭ* is not applied] after the roots *sṛp*, *sṛj*, *spṛś*, *sphūrj*, *svarati*, and *smarati*.
103. And [the augment *iṭ* is not applied] after *goṣan* and others.
The *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) occurs after the prefixes *adhi* and *abhi* before the root *skand*, 104;
after *pari* before the root *stṛ*, 105;
and also when a *repha* (*r*) follows [the prefix], 106.
"May we overcome those who attack us.
(107) Thus ends the second chapter.
"Sahāvān," at the end, is long. (1)
1. [The substitution of *a* occurs] for the final vowel of the eight items beginning with *pada*, *yoga*, *pakṣa*, *parṇa*, *daṃṣṭra*, and *cakra*.

2. [The substitution of *a* occurs] for the final vowel of a word ending in *vyadha* when followed by the suffix *apratyaya*. 3. [The substitution of *a* occurs] for the final vowel of a word ending in *uñ* when followed by the words *idam*, *ūṣu*, and so forth. 4. [The substitution of *a* occurs] for the final vowel of a word ending in *uñ* when followed by the words *ūṣu*, and so forth.
Oṣadhe, apa-ñca-padyām (5);
jīvantīm oṣadhīm (6);
sāḍhaḥ (7).
8. Abundantly during the night;
9. Of the universe among men, wealth, and friends;
10. At the foot of the dog.
11. The vowel of a verbal prefix ending in a non-nasal consonant is lengthened before a root beginning with *d*.
12. [The vowel of a root] such as *vṛt* and others [is lengthened] in these cases.
13. The vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is frequently [lengthened].
The forms *jihīḍāham*, *sāhyāma*,
and *vidmā* occur in place of [the expected forms] in verses beginning with *śara*.
The third case ending is generally used for the object of the mental faculty (matau) and of desire (icchāyām), provided that the following word begins with the letter *y*. (17–19)
20. When there is elision of *ra*, [the rule applies] to the first [group], namely *nāraka* and so forth; 21. to the second [group], namely *dīdāya* and so forth; 22. [and likewise to others].

23. Of *sātrāsāha* and others, the first vowel of the second member [is pluta]. 24. [The first vowel of the second member is pluta] before *ṛta*, *vṛdha*, and *varīvāne*. 25. Also [the first vowel of the second member is pluta] before *tyam*, *dhīḥ*, and *para*, with the exception of *vara*.

A consonant at the end of a word is doubled (26). The letters ṅ, ṇ, and n, when preceded by a short vowel, are doubled before a vowel (27). A consonant at the beginning of a conjunct (saṃyoga), following a vowel, is doubled (28).
The *visarjanīya* is not [elided]; 29. and when followed by a letter of the same class; 30. and the letters *ra* and *ha* follow those two. 31.
The sounds ś, ṣ, and s remain unchanged before a vowel (32); pragṛhya vowels also remain unchanged (33);
and so do enā, ehā, and others (34).
35. When *yava* is elided, [the preceding vowel remains].
36. A solitary *u*-vowel preceded by a vowel [remains].
37. In the case of *namaḥ*, there is a euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*).

The simple vowel *ā* is first [substituted] for the preceding [vowel] (38); a semi-vowel is the final element of a vowel-ending [stem] (39); and *ay*, *av*, and *āv* are the substitutes for the diphthongs (39).
41. One [vowel] replaces both the preceding and the following [vowels].
42. A long vowel replaces a homogeneous vowel before another homogeneous vowel.
43. In the word *sīmanta*, [the vowel] becomes short.
The *e* vowel replaces the *a* vowel before an *i* vowel; 44.
the *o* vowel replaces the *a* vowel before an *u* vowel; 45. [the *a* vowel is replaced] by *ara* or *am* before an *ṛ* vowel; 46.
And in the case of *uparṣanti* and others; 47.
The *ṛ* of a prefix becomes *ā* before the initial *dhātu* (root); 48. And [it becomes *ā*] in the case of a past participle used as an instrument; 49.
The vowel *ai* arises from the combination of *e* and *i*; 50. the vowel *au* arises from the combination of *o* and *u*; 51.
according to Śākalya and others, there is elision (*lopa*) of the subsequent [vowel] in these cases. 52.
53. Before a word-initial *a*, [the final] *e* or *o* [becomes *ai* or *au*]. 54. In some cases, there is the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). 55.
When *e* or *o* at the end of a word is followed by an *a*, that [resulting *ai* or *au*] is called *abhinihita*.
The two *ik* vowels [of *jñā* and *ti*] are fused (*praśliṣṭa*). 56.

After a word preceded by an *anudātta* vowel and ending in a consonant cluster beginning with a semivowel (*saṃyoga-ādi-yavanta*), the subsequent [vowel] is *svarita*, or optionally the preceding one, as in *jñātyaḥ*. 57. When an *antasthā* (semivowel) follows an *udātta* vowel and is followed by an *anudātta* vowel, it is called *kṣaipra*. 58.
59. Also within a word, [the substitution of *u* occurs] in the case of *pañcapadyā*. 60. Everywhere, [the substitution of *u* occurs] for the vowel *ū*.
61. And [the substitution of *u* occurs] for *oṇ*.
*Tairovyañjana* occurs when [a vowel] is separated by consonants;
*pādavṛtta* occurs in the case of a hiatus (*vivṛtti*); *savidha* occurs in the case of an *avagraha*. 62–64.
The *nihata* (elided) vowels—namely the *abhinihita*, *prāśliṣṭa*, *jāti*, *ajaipra*, and *prāṇa*—which follow an *udātta* or a *svarita*, have a duration of one-sixteenth of a *mātrā*;
the wise call this *vikampita*. 65.
When a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) arises from the meeting of an *udātta* vowel with another, it is *udātta*. 66.

An unaccented vowel following an acute accent is marked with a svarita (circumflex) accent. This applies even in the case of Vyāsa (word-division), provided the vowels belong to the same word, as well as in the case of an avagraha.
70. [An *anudātta* syllable] is not [subject to this change] when followed by an *udātta* or a *svarita*.
71. An *anudātta* following a *svarita* has the sound of an *udātta*. 72. This also applies in the case of separation (*vyāsa*), even within the same word (*samānapada*).
And in the case of an avagraha [73]; a non-udātta vowel following a svarita or udātta vowel [74];
and within the same word, *n* becomes *ṇ* after *ṛ*-vowels, *r*, and *ṣ* [75].
76. [The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs] after a word ending in a consonant within a compound, when followed by *drughaṇa* and so forth.

77. [The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs] for the final *n* of the word *ahan* when it ends in *a*. 78. [The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs] for the final *n* of a case-ending, an augment, or the end of a nominal stem.

The study of the Veda is the duty (dharma) for one who desires the state of luminosity after death; it is to be performed by those skilled in sacrifice exactly as it has been handed down in the traditional recensions.
The collection of sacrifices is not separate from the Vedas (104);
moreover, the worlds are established upon sacrifice (105);
and the five classes of people are within the worlds (106).

The study of individual words (pada-pāṭha) is for the purpose of knowing the meanings of words beginning with "anta" and so forth, as well as their accents; 107. Furthermore, the modification of accents (*svaropajana*) in both the *pada* and the *saṃhitā* serves an unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭa*). 109.

There are two types of word-breaks: the break at the end of a line (kramapada) and the break at the end of a section (tasyāntena). The connection with what follows occurs at the end of that [section]. A word ending in a pause is not joined with what follows.
